maintopic: DEATH OF HER ROYAL HIGHNESS THE DUCHESS OF CONNAUGHT.
DEATH OF HER ROYAL HIGHNESS THE DUCHESS OF CONNAUGHT.

speechtext:
On the Orders of the Day:
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE E. FOSTER: I should like to call the attention of the House briefly, and I hope fittingly, to a sad event which has occurred since the House adjourned. I allude to the death of Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Connaught, who passed away on the 14th of March at Clarence House in London after a brief illness. I very well remember the beautiful autumn day on which His Royal Highness and the Duchess of Connaught made their entry into the capital city of the Dominion, passing along in front of the old Parliament Building, and on to their new home farther down on the banks of the Ottawa. Her Royal Highness was by person entirely unknown to us at that time, bht she was heartily welcomed as the consort of the soldier son of the well beloved Queen Victoria. As the wife of a soldier whom she accompanied on his journeyings around the Empire she became known to all, and her grace and dignity endeared her to the hearts .of British subjects the wide world over., Her Royal Highness eooin, entered, dinto the life of Gaimad-a, quietly but with zest. Canadian sports and social activities attracted her attention, atid participation. Local charities, and the wider charities of the provinces and of the Dominion claimed her devotion. In all of these she participated unobtrusively, kindly, and effectively. The war brought about a situation very trying to Her Royal Highness, in that the land of her birth was involved in hostility to the land of her adoption. Her Royal High-

ness ably seconded the untiring efforts of the Duke of Connaught in everything that had for its object the welfare and comfort of the soldier, whether in Canada or at the front, and more particularly those whose lot it was, in the fortunes of war, to become prisoners in a hostile country. Great charities were inaugurated or helped by Her Royal Highness, and which, owing to her strong sympathy and tactful manner, were crowned with success. On leaving Canada in October, 1916, after a sojourn here of almost five years, she continued to go about doing good in London and its vicinity, the soldiers chiefly being the object of 'solicitude, and more particularly those from the country of her five years' sojourn. She has passed away, but not from our memories. Her singular directness of manner, her innate kindness, the personal touch which she seemed to give to her acquaintanceship and her friendships, remain with us. When the news of her death came across the ocean it left us all with a sense of personal loss. I think I may take it upon myself to say that I am voicing the opinion of this Parliament and of the people of Canada in asking this House to convey to His Royal Highness and to the family so sadly bereaved our deepest and most heartfelt sympathy.

maintopic: DEATH OF HER ROYAL HIGHNESS THE DUCHESS OF CONNAUGHT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the House of Commons will, I km sure, aviail themselves of this, the first opportunity at their disposal, to express their deep sense of reverence for the memory of the noble lady who for five years was associated with the life of this country. Every word that has fallen from the lips of my right hon. friend is true to the very letter. The memory of Her Royal Highness will ever be cherished by the Canadian people, who had learned to appreciate her many noble qualities. As has been observed by my right hon. friend, Her Royal Highness was of a retiring and unobtrusive disposition. The duties of her office, whether public or private, she carried out in a most admirable manner, never sparing herself so far as her health would permit. Notwithstanding her ill health, which prevented her during her residence in Canada from participating to the extent she would wish in philanthropic and social duties, the people of Canada had opportunity to appreciate to some extent her kindness of heart and her beneficence. It was her fate, as has been observed by my right hon. friend, to have the last years of her life 
saddened by this terrible war between two countries to which she was bound by such close ties. It is written that a daughter will leave the house of her father to follow her husband. This Her Royal Highness did. When she wedded a son of Queen Victoria she was not only wedded to the life of her husband but also to his country. No one within the wide -range of the British Empire could suffer more than she, the agony that has resulted from this war. Her heart ever beat true to the cause of her adopted, country. I 'hope (that our expression of to-day will convey to her husband and to her children some -consolation in the knowledge that her memory will ever endure in the hearts of the people of Canada.

maintopic: DECLARATION OF WAR BY THE UNITED STATES.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: DECLARATION OF WAR BY THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I wish Mr. Speaker to allude to an event of very great importance, namely, the entrance of the United States of (America into (the war which for nearly three years now has plagued the world -and ihas iraged with unexampled destructiveness. Yesterday the British Parliament passed a resolution affirming their appreciation and gratefully recognizing the fact that at this supreme juncture the United States had elected to take its place on the side of the Allies, in vindication of the cause of right, and justice, and freedom for which the Allies have so long been fighting. While there are many considerations which attach to such action by the United States when its President made his memorable address on the second of April, there are some which make it peculiarly important and peculiarly fateful. The United States, for a hundred years and more, by its traditions and its practice had kept almost completely aloof from European wars and contentions. It had -enjoyed for a century uninterrupted peace with outside powers of great strength. It had successfully passed through a period of internal struggle, the greatest which ever fell to the lot of a nation. The result of that struggle was to reaffirm freedom; and in the succeeding years the North and the South, at one time rent apart by this internal war, had been welded together in peace, - concord, and union. The country s traditions, its history, its pacific pursuits, its geographical position, the allocation of its popu-

lation with so many millions dwelling at a distance from the sea-coast and far from the menace or the allurements of possible warfare, had bred in its people a spirit of antagonism to war itself, and particularly to war , in which the 'territorial possessions or the general rights of the nation were not attacked or infringed upon. When the German hordes smashed through Belgium defying its guaranteed immunity from invasion, a sentiment was violated which was possibly as strong in the United States of America as in any other country. The developments of the war, from the first- outbreak until it included virtually the whole world, involved in many cases the defiance of principles of international action and of humanitarianism which were held dear by the people of the United States. Yet for two years and a half that nation maintained its position of neutrality, maintained it honestly, maintained it thoroughly, even under conditions of great provocation and difficulty. The United States had no territory to gain by entering into the war, it had no- selfish motives so far as power territorial or political was concerned. It stood as a great neutral power, carefully noting the trend and development of the war; protesting on one side and on the other at the violation or infringement of rights. But at last the nation came to the conclusion that it could no longer remain neutral, and it felt compelled to throw its ' weight of one hundred millions of peace-loving, liberty-loving, democratic people with the cause of the Allies.
To my mind, outside of any armies which the United States may gather, drill, and send to a fighting front; outside of any aid which can be given toy her fleet, now large and capable of being made much larger and more powerful; outside of any strength which she may bring to this contest by virtue of her resources, the supremest effect of the entrance of the United States into this war is that in the gradual clarifying of the issues she came to the conclusion that the moral and international sanctions were against the Germans and in favour of the Allies. It is something when such a nation, trying by every possible means to avoid entrance upon the arena, finds itself at last compelled by virtue of its high traditions of morality, humanitarianism and regard for international rights, to come to the conclusion that it can stay . out no longer, but must throw its sword into the scale in favour of democracy, of justice, and of the liberties of small nations.
39J
That, to my mind, is the greatest factor which the entrance of the United States imports into this contest, and history, I believe, will so record it.
As was voiced yesterday in the Mother of Parliaments, in both branches, the United States brings at once, by the position she has taken, a wealth of and a quickly utilizable power of resource, which is of immense benefit to the allied forces in this war against Germany. I think sometimes we can easily make the mistake of not properly understanding and adequately weighing the immense drain upon the warring nations in blood and resources during the last two years and eight months. France stood to her trenches week after week, month after month, year after year, to beat back the millions of her enemies who already had desecrated and destroyed one-itenith of her territory and were seeking to wreak upon the other nine-tenths the same vengeance and destruction. France did not def that without the shedding of blood almost without parallel, without a drain upon her resources of moral and human fibre that cannot be calculated and which cannot be portrayed by pencil or by tongue. If that be true in reference to France, it is measureably true with the other warring nations and allies. Great Britain herself, who has taken a tremendous part in this contest both by sea and by land, who has borne the brunt of practically the whole of the burden by sea, has within two years made out of her peace-loving citizens, an army that in number, in calibre, in courage and in skill in armed warfare, has never been surpassed by the soldiers of any nation however long they may have been trained and drilled in the exercises of war. Great Britain has felt the drain, and felt the drain in a way which we, who are so far distant from the scene of action, find it difficult to have adequate conception of.
Leaving that argument to apply to all the forces which have been in this war for these two years and eight months, what an immense thing it is that new resources, virgin and untouched, new resources in material and new resources in men, come now upon the theatre of this contest to take their vital and strong part in the ultimate decision that has been so long and so destructively fought for on all the fronts in this war.
It not only imparts courage to the soldiers who have been long warring, but it gives actual sustenance, food, munitions and support in a way in which these things were not given before at a time when they

are badly needed, and in the way of finance itself-moneys which make it possible for Russia, Italy, France, if not for Great Britain herself, to go forward in the remaining months of the war with a feeling of confidence and trust that financial resources will not be failing them, and that in these last decisive months of the war what the United States has to give in that respect will be to a large extent determining factors in the result that shall be attained.
If we come down to the actual forces now in the field, Great Britain's experience is rich and ripe and will be availed of. Great Britain sent her whole standing army in the early part of the war into France. The men who were the fighters in the ranks were the officers and trainers of the fighters who took part in the gallant contests in France and Belgium which ultimately resulted in the victory of the Marne, suffered a great depletion in their ranks. There was not only the loss of actual numbers, but the loss as [DOT]well of those officers and trained men who were fitted for training the soldiers to take the vacant places in the depleted ranks of that first British army. The United States to-day could possibly send a good, well-organized little army to the front, but if they did they would deprive themselves of those very factors which are necessary to the early and complete training of that large army which in the end might be effective. So that, we come down to the conclusion that, with all the wisdom that has been gained from the past, and having regard to all the necessities of the situation, a large army from the United States cannot find its way to the battle front for eight, or nine, or twelve months at the very least. But, even though that be so, that might be the very time at which the coming of a new, fresh army of a million or two million might be the deciding factor in the war.
We do not know when this war shall cease. It is endless, its lengthening out has paralyzed the thought and conception of all men who thought about it and its possible time of conclusion. Three months [DOT]-six months we said; nine months, a year, we said; and yet two years and eight months have passed their long, dreary and sanguinary length and there is no man who can tell how long this gigantic struggle may yet last. If it turns out that this war, holding all these different points of vantage, works its weary length along for another year, with the increasing exhaustion of the Allies and enemy forces, then the importation of a fresh, virile force of a mil-
[Slr George Poster.]
lion or two millions of men spells absolute victory for the side upon which it fights and absolute defeat for the side against which it fights. I think it was Count Reventlow, who, after two years of cogitation, in a sentence or two, placed the issue ' between the two parties pretty accurately when he said: There is a necessity for victory for Germany or it will spell the downfall of the German monarchy. That is really the clarified issue to-day-the democracies of the world are at war with the autocratic bureaus and kaisers of the world and the ultimate grinding down of the whole issue must be this: That in Germany the people must rule, and only by a victory of the Allies does it seem possible that the results which we are fighting for can be won.
The United States entered upon this undertaking not yet a month ago and with characteristic energy it is preparing in a scientific and energetic way. It has the wide and sometimes bitter, experience of the nations which have been warring from which to get its information so that it may avoid the mistakes, and at the same time avail of those things which have been most effective. The United States having entered into this war, and living up to the declaration of its president, will without doubt carry out the work to which it has set itself with the same characteristic energy and, we trust, with the same success as has characterized 'the efforts of the other allied nations. To us who live here, along a border of 4,000 miles, neighbours in peace for a hundred years now with the people to the south of us, it is very gratifying that our neighbours, with whom we are upon such good terms and with whom we have so much to do, have agreed with us in our conception of the rights of the issues in this warfare and have now joined with us, and with the other defenders of those rights, in pushing the war to a successful conclusion and in bringing about an era when the democracies of the world shall enjoy the freedom and peace to which they are entitled.

maintopic: DECLARATION OF WAR BY THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
JMr. Speaker, the entrance of the United States into this world-wide war introduces a new chapter not only into the history of the United States itself, but into the history of the world. If, in the month of August 1914, any citizen of the United States had ventured to predict that in this conflict the United States itself would take
t

a part, that man, at that time, would not have been taken seriously. Many people indeed outside of the United States, and perhaps also within the United States, were sorry, when the neutrality of Belgium was invaded, that the United States did not raise its powerful voice to at least protest against that outrage. But such a course of action would not have been in accordance with the traditions of the Republic. The founders of the American nation had hoped, and indeed they in solemn terms .warned their people, that they should forever keep away from the conflicts of Europe. They had hoped that the young nation which had just had its birth, would initiate a new civilization which would furnish an example to the rest of the world, and that as far as they were concerned they would live at peace with every nation. But, they had counted without regard to the march of events, the discoveries of science, the facilities of locomotion and communication which have brought the nations of the earth very close to One another. The principle has at last found expression in the United States itself that no nation which pretends to be civilized can keep outside the pale of civilization, that there is a solidarity amongst all nations and that the law of might against right cannot go unchallenged. Therefore, they have thrown their sword into the balance.
[Some people, in fact many people, have found fault with what they called the hesitation of- the President. We in this House and in this country do not share those views. President Wilson has acted with great caution; he has acted with great prudence; but at the same time he has,always maintained high ideals of the civilization of the world. He had to contend not only with the German element in the population of the Republic, but also with' the great body of pacifists who hoped against all hope that they would forever keep their country free from the bane of war. But by the course he has pursued the President has at last brought the whole of the American people, almost without exception, to stand 'behind him in support of the cause of the Allies. No more than this could be expected from that nation. I share in everything that has been said by my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster).
We do not know when thie war will end. We all hope that it will end even before the American Army is called upon to fight. If it is called upon to fight, then there can be no doubt as to the issue. But we hope
that the issue will be decided even before the armies of the United States cross the sea, and that the weight of their moral action alone will be a decisive factor in favour of victory. We, more than any other part of the British Empire, more than any other part of the civilized world, are interested in the. action which has just been taken by the United States. We share with them this continent. We hope that henceforth, as a result of this war, the solidarity of the nations will be established; not only that the solidarity of nations will be established but that the brotherhood of man will be the basis of the future relationships of the world. Let us hope that thie brotherhood of man with -man will commence in our relationship with the United States. There were some men amongst us who were afraid of too close relations with the United States. We have no such fear on one side of the House at all events, and I am glad to say that now there is not much fear on the other side either. My hon. friends on the other side now realize that there are no dregs in the cup of freedom, that it is wholesome to the last drop. Free wheat has come about as the result of the present situation. I shall not dilate upon this point, it may come up for discussion later on; but upon the present occa-
4 p.m. sion I join my voice most gladly in everything that has been said by my right hon. friend.
On the Orders of the Day:

Would the Acting Prime Minister inform us if the report in the press of this morning is true, that the Right Hon. Mr. Balfour and General Joffre are to be officially invited by the Government to visit Canada?
I do not know the source of my hon. friend's information
The Ottawa morning papers.

I shall be better able to answer that question in the course of a day or two than at present. In the meantime, my hon. friend may rest assured that it would be a source of the greatest possible satisfaction to us if we could prevail upon Mr. Balfour and his distinguished colleagues on that Commission, when they have coipe to this side of the water, to pay Canada a visit.
Hear, hear.

There is this other consideration, that it is a wonderful thing that such men in such positions could have taken the time to have crossed the Atlantic-to say nothing of the perils of the crossing-out of the midst of the business of this war, and it is very likely that they will want to get back again just as quickly as their most urgent business will permit.
On the Orders of the Day:

The Minister of Labour to-day referred to the fact that previous to the adjournment of the House in February he had been absent from the House for some time in connection with labour matters in the West; and the House will recall that the Premier announced that on his return the minister would give to the House a statement as to what he had done in the West in regard to adjusting the difficulties which had arisen in connection with the mining situation there. I understand that while in the West the minister made some arrangement of a character which assured the temporary resumption of work by the men; but I see the following dispatch in yesterday's paper:
Calgary, April 17.-The coal miners of nearly every mine of the district are out on strike because of the delay in the settlement of the men's affairs.
The ranks of idle miners were augmented this morning by the other places in the Crow's Nest Pass country going out.
The miners now out are at Michel, Blair-more, Canmore, Hillcrest, Bellevue, and Frank.
Those at Drumheller also are out, but the difficulty in the latter company is of a different nature.
The minister is well aware that this subject is of very great importance and is regarded as such not only by the men interested but by labour everywhere. I would ask the minister to give to the House a statement such as was promised by the Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):

speechtext: Who?

Mr. Harrison, fair wage officer, whose headquarters are at Calgary. He did not complete the inquiry until some time in January, when the operators refused to contribute any money towards this increase in the cost of living. The immediate conditions -were worse, in a sense, than they had been in November. I went out in the latter part of January, when the thermometer registered 48 degrees below zero. Intense suffering would follow if these coal mines were closed up. Hon. gentlemen know that the domestic coal used in the West does not endure for any length of time unless it is very carefully stored, it disintegrates, slackens and becomes useless. Generally speaking, no large stocks
of coal, therefore, are kept on hand for domestic purposes, and the closing of these mines for a few days would mean great suffering. The operators refused to do anything. It was found by the Commissioner that the increase in the cost of living was equivalent to $1.75 a week in wages. In order that the mines might be continued, I undertook that we would check up the amount that would be payable to these miners at the rate of $1.75 per week from and after the 15th of November until the 4th of February, and that we would advance that amount in the first instance and take our chances of getting it back from the larger consumers, several of whom had undertaken to pay, for the coal shipped to them during that period, a sum equivalent to this $1.75 in addition to the price that they had arranged to pay for it. The operators undertook to pay that $1.75 per week from and after the 3rd of February until the 1st of April when the current agreement would expire. This agreement provides that thirty days before its expiration, which would be the '31st of March, the operators and the representatives of the miners should meet together and endeavour to negotiate a new agreement to become effective on the first of April, this proviso being intended to prevent a cessation of work at the end of the period covered by the agreement, as had occurred three or four times previously. A conference was held at Calgary early in March, but the operators felt that the new demands made by the miners were so great that there was no probability of any understanding being reached. I went out there and spent nine days with them, and two weeks ago last Monday I succeeded in inducing them to appoint a sub-committee of four representatives of the operators and * four representatives of the miners, which sub-committee has been in session ever since. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has referred to some of the mines in which the men have gone out on strike. My advice is that they have done so as their protest against the protracted negotiations going on at Calgary. They have got the impression that the operators and the miners should have reached a conclusion earlier. The last word I received in regard to the matter was from my officer at Calgary who said it was expected that the joint conference of operators and miners would to-day report a conclusion reached by this sub-committee. I have no doubt the conclusion will be accepted by the operators, but it will have to be submitted

to the miners of the different mines throughout that district for their approval. If, as is anticipated, an agreement is reached to the satisfaction of the gentlemen representing the miners, I am confident that they will induce the miners to accept it and that there will he no further trouble.

How much money
has the Government paid out in conset-quence of the undertaking given by the minister to make up this difference in regard to the cost of living? ' Has the Minister received from the parties who have got the coal anything to compensate the Government for the disbursement, and if so, how much?

It has been a very
slow process to get the reports as to the quantifies that have been shipped to different people, but the amount paid out by the Government is about $92,000, and I believe that we shall receive every dollar of it.
How much have you received now?

We have not seceived any. The time has not arrived for its return. The other day I wrote to the president of a company in the United States which had received 41,000 tons from one mine, pointing out to him the arrangement that had been made and telling him that we expected his company to contribute. I was very much gratified at his prompt reply: "Certainly, we will contribute whatever is said to be right." It was thought that contributions should be 25 cents per ton, and that is what I believe the operators have added to their prices from and after the 3rd of February to cover the payment of $1.75 per week. Three or four of the larger consumers agreed to contribute before we undertook to advance the money, so that I do not think the Government will lose a dollar in the matter.
Was the payment provided for by a special Order in Council, and, if so, would the minister bring down the Order in Council and any other papers relating to the matter?
The money was advanced under the authority of an Order in Council, and I shall be glad to bring it down.
Would the minister say if the conference sitting at Calgary has relation to the domestic coal mines or to the steam coal mines?
It has relation to all the mines, the lignite mines as well as the bituminous mines, to all the members of the association operating in District 18, or about twenty mines.
Is it the domestic miners that are making trouble or the steam coal miners?

Most of the domestic coal is produced at the Galt mine at Lethbridge, and the men there are working. There is another mine at Bankhead, where domestic coal is produced chiefly, and the men there are also working. I do not think that lignite coal is produced at any of the mines where the men are out at the present time.
The position is that it is not the domestic coal mines, the mines upon which the prairie farmer or dweller depends for his coal, that are being shut down.
Not at the present time.
It is the mines that provide the steam and smelting coal.

But they were all
involved last winter. They all belong to the same association. I am not sure that any of the mines producing lignite coal are shut down, but I rather think not.

Mr. Speaker, this discussion is all more or less in violation of the rules of the House, and I do not wish to aggravate that condition, but I hope the House will pardon me for saying, in connection with this discussion, that I was yesterday in conference with representatives of the mining industries of Cobalt and Porcupine and the adjacent camps, and they feel that trouble is coming in that quarter, their view, and probably that of a large number of the people of this country, being that labour strikes in connection with mining ought in a time of war to be dealt with under the War Measures Act, if we have one, in the way that similar strikes have been dealt with in England. Such strikes have been anticipated there in this way, and as a consequence they have not occurred. We ought to find a way, in the state of war that obtains in Canada to-day, of approaching these mining labour troubles before they reach a head and if possible preventing a strike occurring. It is not a hard thing to do. The War Measures method must be adopted by Parliament and this Government in connection with the failure of our railways to deliver coal and

freight of other kind to onr cities, in particular to the manufacturing cities of Ontario.

In reply to my hon.
friend, I would say that no other country in the world that I am aware of has had so few labour troubles as Canada has had in the last few years. Australia is sometimes referred to. Last year, with only two-thirds of our population, they had four times the number of strikes we had, and so with the United States and with England. Things are not just as we would like to have them in Canada in this respect, but our wage-earners have shown up well in the matter Of freedom from strikes.

subtopic: BAY AND STE. ANNE DE BEAUPRE.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: BAY AND STE. ANNE DE BEAUPRE.
speechtext: I am sorry that the Minister of Railways has left the House, but perhaps some other member of the Government will bring to his attention the question I desire to ask. It was reported a few days ago that the branch line of the Intercolonial from Rivibre Ouelle would be discontinued and a new service inaugurated on the north shore of the river between Murray Bay and Ste. Anne de Beaupre, running through Ste. Irenes to Ste. Anne de Beaupre and connecting up with the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway. One report said that the rails of this branch line had already been carried over to the other 6ide to be used on the Quebec and Saguenay line. I sent a telegram to the Minister of Railways, and another to the Minister of Inland Revenue, whom I am happy to see in the House, and four days later the Minister of Inland Revenue informed me that the report was erroneous and without foundation. But since that time the new service has practically been advertised in the ministerial papers of the province. Yesterday, in La Patrie, of Montreal, the fare between Murray Bay and Quebec was announced. I think-the people of the district are entitled to know the intention of the Government in this matter.

subtopic: BAY AND STE. ANNE DE BEAUPRE.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways is out of the chamber at the moment, but I shall see him directly, and will give my hon. friend the information he desires to-morrow.

subtopic: BAY AND STE. ANNE DE BEAUPRE.
speechtext:
I would ask that the information be made public, because many people are interested in this service. In
addition to what my hon. friend from Kamouraska has pointed out, there is a large colony of Americans, who come up every year to spend the summer at Murray Bay and in the neighbouring district, who would be very much inconvenienced if they were deprived of this valuable service.

subtopic: BAY AND STE. ANNE DE BEAUPRE.
speechtext: They will be soldiering this summer.

I would point out that according to Rule 17 (c) the House has no Supply ready to take to-day. I would not make any objection because we might take Civil Government Estimates as we have done before, but as we got the Auditor General's Report only the other day, we are not in a position to take Civil Government Estimates now.
It is Civil Government that we propose to go on with, if my right hon. friend has no objection.
I would suggest that we take it up to-morrow. I will raise no objection then.

The House again proceeded to consideration of the motion of Mr. R. Bickerdike (Montreal, St. Lawrence) for the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Criminal Code and to abolish capital punishment.
He said: Since the House adjourned there have been a number of occurrences bearing on this question, one of the most important of which is the fact that Russia in the last week of the month of March abolished capital punishment, and I hope that this Parliament will at an early date pass a resolution congratulating them on having abolished not only capital punishment, but also the Romanoff dynasty. Another important occurrence was the sentencing to death of a young boy of sixteen in Manitoba. I did not think it was possible to find in this country a judge or a jury that would condemn a child to be hanged. However, such is the case. This boy is to be hanged on the 15th of May. A large number of petitions have been circulated throughout the country asking for clemency, not only to save the life of this young boy, but to save this young nation

from the everlasting disgrace of hanging a child of sixteen. If there is one thing on which we all are agreed it is the fact that women and children should be exempt from hanging in Canada. We have had several mass meetings in different places in the province of Quebec, one in Montreal and another in Sherbrooke, and with the permission of the House I shall read the following resolution, which was passed at a meeting of the citizens of Montreal, held in the Windsor Hall on Monday evening, April 2, 1917, and which is identical with the resolutions passed at the other meetings:
BE IT RESOLVED, That whereas there now lies within the Dominion of Ca'.uni \ & young lad of sixteen under the condemnation of death and whose father is at the present moment fighting with his regiment in the British army in Prance in defence of the Empire; and
WHEREAS this meeting has heard read a petition addressed to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada praying for the commutation of his sentence of death to one of imprisonment:
BE IT RESOLVED that it is the sense of this meeting that the infliction of the death penalty is contrary to the dictates of civilization and Christianity, and we hereby protest against the proposed hanging of this young boy of the tender years of sixteen and which we consider would be a blot on the fair name of the Dominion of Canada;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that copies of this resolution he forwarded to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada and all members of the Dominion Parliament.
If we cannot all agree that capital punishment should be abolished entirely at this time, we can surely all agree that the day has gone by for hanging women and children. And I hope that every member of this House will have an opportunity to declare by his vote Whether he is in favour oi hanging this boy or not.
Does the hon. gentleman object to shooting?
I do.
Then, he must object to the war?
I do.
Gracious, this is terrible.

If I had to shoot the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burnham) I would, as the Irishman says, only wing him, not kill him.
When the House adjourned on January 31st, I was about to say that in the early days I had had my attention called to the

brutal and inhuman practice of hanging in this and other countries whose citizens lay claim to being quite civilized and generally as enlightened as those of other communities, where this horrible practice of the Middle Ages has long since been abolished. Having first been actuated by sentiment in my opposition to the infliction of the death penalty, I began to read upon the subject, and from being an opponent on the ground that it was brutal and inhuman, I finally have come to the further belief that the question is one of government, as it relates to the safety of life and the more certain and unerring enforcement of law.
In presenting an argument in support of these measures for the abolishment of capital punishment, I have endeavoured to show that the main defence in support of the death penalty inflicted by .the state, to wit: that its infliction is a prevention of crime and therefore insures greater safety of life, is wholly and absolutely in error. I have endeavoured also to show that the example set by the state in taking human life, is at once brutalizing and demoralizing; that it has a strong tendency to destroy in the breasts of men the sense of the sacredness of life; and that it acts as a dangerous suggestion to the vicious mind. I have endeavoured to show that in communities where the death penalty is not inflicted, life is quite as secure, as there is far more certainty of conviction than in communities where capital punishment is enforced. For the purpose of setting forth the best possible data upon this subject, I have used statistics and quotations taken from numerous and well informed authorities.
We are told that " Whoso sheddeth man's blood, 'by man shall his blood be shed." This is quite true, but it has nothing to d.o with the penal laws of to-day. Moses may have decreed that " Witches shall be put to death," but because of this there is no reason why any statute should exist today perpetuating this decree. Moses may have laid down that if A destroys B's eye, then shall A have his own eye burst or excised, or that if A breaks B's tooth, then shall a dental surgeon be told .off to draw a similar tooth of his. Because a certain code of laws was suitable for a nomadic people many thousands of years ago, it is absurd to quote them as having binding force today under very, different conditions.
Capital punishment by legal statutes has been an institution rock-buttressed, respected, protected and even fawned upon by the elect as one of the indispensable pillars of

a righteous and self-respecting government. The following are the names of some who have declared against the death penalty: Abraham Lincoln, Senator Sherman, Roscpe Conkling, Horatio Seymour, Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes, A. B. Richmond, Wendell Phillips. Catherine, Empress of Russia, said, " We must punish crime without imitating it. The punishment by death is rarely anything but a useless barbarity." Elizabeth, another of the Russian empresses, said:	" Experience demonstrates
that capital punishment never yet made man better." The Right Hon. John Bright said:
Whenever you hang a man in the face of the public under the circumstances to which we are so accustomed, if you do in the slightest degree deter from crime by the shocking nature of the punishment, I will undertake to say that you, by so much, may by much more, weaken that very and greater security which arises from the reverence with which human life is regarded.
The State does not kill people merely hecause they are worthless and to be rid >f them. Insane asylums are built at great expenses for the incurable, upon whom relatives cannot bear to look, who personally may be better off dead. The State tenderly cares for all such cases. This is done because the example of kindness and humanity to the unfortunate is of an inestimable benefit to society. A man would 'be 'a brute 

lower than the dogs that devoured the body of Jezebel-who would say, kill them to be rid of these imbecile burdens. It is not possible to imagine the effect society would feel if we were to destroy all imbeciles and the incurable insane. What a horrible example would be set for the people of the State to follow. No calculation could be made of the injury to the morals of the State by countenancing such conduct. One of the greatest advantages t.o the State from the preservation and tender care and treatment of the hopeless insane is this example of humane treatment and of tender consideration of a human life however useless and pitiable it may seem. Our citizens are taught to be kind and gentle to the unfortunate by this example of the State.
As professors of the religion of Jesus Christ, we find no sanction in the record of His life and teachings to the shedding of human blood by judicial process. The whole trend of His example and precept was in the direction of love for the whole brotherhood of man.

Was i)ot He sacrificed
in o/der that the word of God might be fulfilled?
Surely.
Well, what is the matter with that?

The only thing the matter with it is that you do n.ot believe it. Revenge and the retaliation had no place in the heart of the Redeemer, and if we are Christians, they can have no place in our hearts, and certainly should not have in the State. As we apprehend, the attitude of the State .towards its criminals should be one of reformation, coupled always with such powerful restraint as will ensure the safety of society. That the substitution of life imprisonment for the death penalty is a step that may be taken with safety is manifest not only from years of successful experience in those States where capital punishment has been abolished, but also in our own country, where we have criminals serving life sentences in the penitentiary, whose crimes were as atrocious as those of others who were executed.
May I now ask the members of this House if they believe any boy sixteen years of age, any mother's son, either black or white, should be hanged? His father is right in the trenches, where our friend came from recently, fighting the battles of the Empire. I have much pleasure in moving the second reading of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Bickerdike) has introduced the same subject on several occasions in this House and, I believe, moved the adoption of practically the same Bill. On each occasion the position assumed by the Government was stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who, unfortunately, is not in the House at present. I believe, however, that my views on the question, never before expressed in Parliament or elsewhere, as far as I remember, coincide in principle with those of the minister and are line for line and precept for precept opposed to those of the hon. member.
Perhaps it would be better for me first to state the points which he has advanced upon which we are in agreement. I agree with the hon. member in this, that in all cases where the crime of murder, or treason, or rape, or any crime punishable by death under the code is committed, it would be inconsistent with the principles

of humanity that the supreme penalty should be exacted. I agree with Mm further that we are not able to justify the exaction of the supreme penalty in any ease by reference to any doctrine merely because such doctrine is laid down in the Mosaic law. But, I cannot carry my agreement with the hon. member for Montreal any further than that. I do not know, if ever, in the course of my life, I bad sympathy with the movement for the abolition of capital punishment, but I do know this, that my experience in the criminal courts in Canada, and my experience later on in connection with the applications for clemency, have driven me from any sympathy that at any time I might have had with the opposition to capital punishment. The hon. member this afternoon endeavoured to get the assent of the House to this modification of his request, namely: if we cannot look for entire abolition, we must at least look for the abolition of the punishment as applicable to children and women. I do not think that the adoption of even that restriction in the absolute could possibly be made. He has referred to a case which is just now, or very shortly will be, before His Royal Highness, that of the convicted murderer Spain from the courts of Manitoba. That was the case where a boy of sixteen, himself not a native of this country, a native of England, murdered in cold blood- and the adjective cannot be too strongly emphasized so far as my information at present goes-two innocent people, two respectable citizens of that province, under most revolting circumstances. It would ill-become me to make any statement-because I do not know all the circumstances, although I know some of them-as to what should be the attitude of the Governor in Council and of His Royal Highness with regard to that case. I have simply to say that the circumstances already made known need only be considered to convince hon. members of this House that if capital punishment is to still remain the final, supreme penalty in the worst cases of murder, it might well be that that case would show that there should be no restriction in its application merely on the score of age. It must be remembered that though the Code lays down the penalty of death as the last supreme penalty that can be exacted in cases of murder, cases of rape and cases of treason, still it is well known everywhere, of course well known in this House and I think well known to juries, in almost every case explained specifically to juries by the [Mr. Meighen 1
trial judges, that there is a prerogative of clemency that still remains, and that the mere finding of a verdict of guilty by no means necessarily entails punishment by death. Consequently the objection raised by my hon. friend this afternoon and at other times has not the force he desires to give it. It is true that juries are more careful, more cautious before they bring in a verdict of guilty in a trial for murder or treason-but particularly in a case of murder where a judge has no option but to impose a penalty of death-than in other cases; and as a consequence it happens no doubt that there are many murderers who escape, proportionately more perhaps than of those who are guilty of other crimes. That may be one of the results that we must suffer by reason of our jurisprudence in this regard. But while juries are more careful, it does not go to the extreme the hon. member fears. Juries are well aware and they are well instructed that the prerogative of clemency lies behind, securely reposing in the Crown; the Crown has power to reduce and to exact only such punishment as to the Crown may 5 p.m. seem mete. The duty upon the judge in case of murder-in other cases it is optional-is imperative; he must, where a verdict of guilty is brought in, himself sentence the prisoner to be hanged. I cannot speak from as wide an experience as perhaps other members of this House, but I can speak from some experience, and I can say that I never knew a jury to whom was committed this awful trust of determining upon the guilt or innocence of a person accused of murder who did not know and who did not admit that they knew that there was a prerogative of mercy, and that their verdict in itself should not mean an irremediable sentence of death. To my mind that disposes in the main of the objection which the. hon. gentleman raises. I am quite willing to admit that the fear, if you may call it so, that the verdict of the jury may result in the taking of a human life does bring on them a caution that sometimes is extreme; that as a consequence perhaps a disproportionate number escape; but I cannot go further and say that the result of that small number, whatever it may be, escaping is anything like so disastrous in relation to the commission of the crime of murder throughout the country as would be the enactment of legislation that would take away the terror and fear of death which deters evi'l-doers. The

Mosaic law must be read with reference to the conditions that existed in Mosaic times; our law must be read with reference to conditions that now obtain. What was necessary then is vital now and that is to see that there is held before the wrongdoer and the criminal such a punishment as bears fitting proportion to the crime he contemplates, and bears a character that becomes the crime he contemplates. It must hot be of such a kind as has been found insufficient to deter even those who contemplate lesser wrongs.
I have been impressed with this as I have walked through jails and prisons on many occasions long* before I entered this House, that the mere punishment by incarceration as incarceration is now in these later days understood and practised, while it has a terror of a character, while it is a punishment of a character and a fitting punishment, would weigh very little in the mind of a man whose lust or greed or passion was so violent or so sordid as would drive him to the taking of human life. It is true that certain portions of civilization, intelligent portions of civilization, have moved beyond the point that we have gone, and have carried the attribute of mercy so far as to abolish capital punishment in every case. But I do not think the movement has been very general. I think this has been a slow movement for many years gone by, and my hon. friend is bound to admit, from instances that have been cited to the House by the minister in other debates, that while it has gone forward and has resulted in the abolition of capital punishment in certain cases, there are many others where it has gone the other way and where public opinion that once went as far as abolition has been reversed and where the old punishment has been restored.
You cannot name one.

I cannot name them, but I think I could name them after very little inquiry. Does the hon. member say that in no state of the Union has a reversal of legislation taken place? That may be, but it does not apply the world over. It may be, as the hon. gentleman says, that there is no state in the American Union that once has abolished capital punishment and later returned to it, but I am quite sure that I myself have read of cases in which countries where they have at one time gone that length and later gone back again.
No country and no state that has abolished capital punishment has ever returned to it.

The 'hon. gentleman
says that it applies to all countries as well as to all states of the Union. I do not think he is correct in that. He may be correct as to the states, but, correct or not, the records do show that in 6ome of the cases, at all events, where the abolition took place the result has not been by any means a diminution of the crime of murder. There might result an increase in the proportion of convictions of murder known to have been committed, 'but cases are undoubtedly recorded in well authenticated works where there has been a pronounced increase in the perpetration of the crime of murder.
Can the hon. gentleman put his finger on a single case or a single statement to that effect? I challenge that statement. I have the facts here.
The hon. gentleman may not have all the facts.
I have sufficient.

While the rules of the House may prevent my speaking again in this debate, the hon. gentleman will introduce his Bill again and we shall have an opportunity of threshing this out. There may be differences of opinion on that point; there may be differences of authority, and the hon. gentleman may have one side and we may have to other; but what appeals to me most of all is this: the character of the punishment must be such as will appeal as a fitting punishment; as will appeal with sufficient terror to the type of man who would contemplate the crime of murder. It would take a great deal of argument to convince me that incarceration as now necessarily practiced can be made eueh a dreaded punishment as will hold in check the passions of men who contemplate the crime of murder. Remember again that in this country-and I believe the same principles apply in the old land and in other countries as well-though the supreme penalty is exacted by law, that is to say, is called for on the part of the bench ae the sentence that must follow conviction for murder, certain well known principles obtain in the execution of that sentence after it is pronounced. One principle I might state is this: it is well known that insanity as defined by the Code, while not a defence, may be pleaded in several ways

and may result in there being no possibility of conviction, because of proven incapacity to commit the crime. But insanity is there defined as insanity in such a degree as in stated degree to paralyse the intellect and prevent the man from knowing in reality the difference between right and wrong. Now, while there may not be incapacitation of intellect to that extent, there may be such a condition of mind, such a lack of development of intellect, such an absence of the full human faculties, as would make it not a fitting case in which to exact the extreme penalty: such a failure fully to appreciate the nature and consequence of the act as, while it would not render the man incapable of committing an act under the definition of the Code, still makes a proper case for interposition on the part of the Crown and of reducing the conviction to imprisonment for a term of years or foi life. That is one principle, and the utmost care is exercised in every case to ascertain whether or not in each individual conviction the prisoner comes within its terms. There are other principles that obtain. It would be impossible for example to deny that if, notwithstanding the verdict of the jury, given in the immediate presence of the witnesses and in the hearing of all the evidence, there should develop other evidence not at the trial producable, or other proper ground to create a reasonable doubt, that reasonable doubt finds interpretation in the decision as to the execution of the penalty. I do not need to pass over again the arguments that have been advanced, much more ably than I can advance them, by the Minister of Justice in previous debates. I think the sense of the House remains pretty much as it was in those previous sessions; I do not know that my own conviction on the subject remains undisturbed by the discussions that have taken place. It would seem to me hard to credit that any one could during many years come in contact with the administration of criminal law and come in contact with the criminal himself as one in the practice of such law must necessarily come, and still believe that there could be as full and adequate prevention of the crime- of murder by any system of imprisonment as there is by the holding out of the possibility of death itself.

My hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) deserves very great credit for the persistence with which he has been bringing forward this Bill year after year against the manifest conviction of the House. His motives

are certainly most honourable, and they are dictated by a cause which everybody appreciates, even if we do not agree with his convictions. To-day, if I understood his observations aright, I thought that he would have been satisfied if the Government had seen its way to accept his Bill partially if not in toto; if the Government had been willing to abolish capital punishment in the case of rape and in the case of murder committed by women and children. At the present time, so far as the first of these is concerned, I do not think that there is any necessity of changing the law. The offence, if I remember aright, is punishable by death or by imprisonment for life or for a period subject to the discretion of the court. The offence is, we are all happy to observe, one of rare occurrence in this country. In the province from which I come, I know of only one conviction during the last fifty years. In that case the prisoner convicted was sentenced, not to death, but to life imprisonment in the penitentiary. Whether he fulfilled his whole term I do not know. As far as crimes committed by women are concerned, in the province from which I come only two sentences have been executed against women during the last sixty years. Undoubtedly there is something revolting in the idea that a woman should be sentenced to death. The member for St. Lawrence must remember the case which occurred in the county of Terrebonne not far from Montreal. The woman was convicted the same time as the person who actually perpetrated the crime. There is no doubt whatever, notwithstanding the sympathy we may have for her case, that of the two she was the more guilty. She enticed a young boy to commit an awful murder, and if there was more guilt on the head of one than on the other, no man could resist the conviction that the woman was the more guilty than the actual perpetrator of the deed. The question as to whether the woman or the actual perpetrator df the deed should be executed is one worthy of consideration. I mention this to my hon. friend simply to show that it is not sufficient to be guided solely by sentiment, and that there may be reasons why the law should be left as it is at present, whether the offender be a man or a woman. I am not aware that a boy has been executed in Canada within the memory of any living man. My hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) and roy hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) have

alluded to the painful case of that boy in Manitoba. So far as we can judge from the reports in the newspapers, it is a horrible case, but I hope there may be redeeming features which will permit the Minister of Justice to report favourably to His Excellency in the matter.
My hon. friend has stated that capital punishment has been abolished in several countries. I do not know whether it is on this occasion or on a previous occasion that he referred to France. Capital punishment, so far as I am aware, has not been abolished in France; but in that country, during the presidency of Mr. Fallieres, it is well known that during the first six years of his seven years tenure of office he would not sign a single sentence of execution, but public opinion at last revolted, and under the powerful force of public opinion President Fallieres had to abandon his own private [DOT] views and at length was compelled to see that the law was carried out.
The matter to which my hon. friend has given his attention, and to which I have no doubt he will give his attention again if the House does not agree with him to-day, is one which has appealed to many thinkers, and we have had very weighty opinions on both sides - of the question, some holding that the death penalty should never be abolished in the case of murder. At the present time, although rape carries with it nominally the penalty of death, with the alternative of imprisonment, no man, no matter what the circumstances are, is sentenced to death for that crime, so that there is no necessity for considering that aspect of the case. But, there has undoubtedly been a sense prevailing in the great majority of the nations of the earth that murder should be punished by death. It is a painful thing to say so; it is a thing against which our instincts revolt; but, after all, if the crime is to be thus punished, I do not know that any serious injustice has taken place. I know that there is no duty which comes within the purview of the Government-I am sure it is the same with the present Government as it was with the last Government-which is more painful than to have to pronounce whether or not a prisoner shall be condemned to death. I am sure that with the present Government, as with the previous Government, the facts of the case are scanned with' great diligence and always with the view, if possible, to find any reason for exercising clemency, and if any reason be found, clemency is recommended to the Governor General. There
are cases, however, so heinous that it is felt that the ends of justice would not be met if the penalty provided by the law were, not carried out.
Whether or not the penalty of death is a deterrent is a much mooted question. Education has more to do with the prevention of crime than even the deterrent effect of the punishment, and in this country it can happily be said that cases of murder are very few in fact, amongst the native population they are becoming less and less frequent. All the cases which have taken place recently have been amongst a class of foreigners who come from a country in which the crime of murder is a daily custom. Without being invidious, I believe that many crimes of that nature have been committed by Italians who came from the south of Italy, where it is the pernicious habit of every man to carry a stiletto. The carrying of weapons is prohibited in this country by law, and I have no doubt that a generation hence these citizens will be just as peaceful and orderly as are our own people. We come, however, always to the same problem: What is the most effective law? Shall we continue the law which we have had on the Statute Book ever since the country has been a country, and which is still the law amongst the most civilized nations of the earth, or shall we be carried away by a feeling of humanity, which is most commendable and most honourable, I admit, but which, after all, will not serve the ends of justice as well as does the present law?

If we believe in God-and I presume the hon. member for St. Lawrence does-God takes away human life through at least His natural instruments. He has arranged it so that the slightest infraction of His law meets with the penalty, and if at any time a deadly sin is committed, that penalty is death. There is no consideration, except perhaps it may be through an abstract principle of the grace of God or some other remote consideration of that kind, such as an analysis of the prompting of the Divine mercy which we cannot consider since they are infinite, and since therefore, they are beyond the grasp of a finite mind, they can be dealt with only in an approximate way. And since they can be dealt with only dn an approximate way, these are matters simply for analysis and not for final decision. Whilst we cann.ot argue about it for the reasons I have given, we can, nevertheless, adopt the means that we see employed by the highest power in carrying out the purposes of the world, and if, therefore, we would imitate the Creator, for a deadly sin we would provide the penalty of death. It must be remembered that there is a very great deal in this which the hon. member has not touched upon. He represents with all his kindness the advanced school of pure utilitarism, that is to say, what, ministers to the general comfort and to the general peace of mind. What is influencing him is what we might call the general well-being in an abstract condition of perfection in humanity That ,s the undercurrent of his thought, and the consideration that is influencing him in bringing forward this measure. Such a consideration as that is absolutely the wrong point of view to take in considering this or any other question founded upon the principles of conduct. It is to deny altogether the priori

and to say that there are no abstract abiding principals in the world which aTe infused into us in some way which we cannot grasp, but which, nevertheless, come to us exactly as the principle of life itself comes to us. We can make nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen and those other things which go to make up the hemoglobin, but we cannot infuse into the compound the vital spark which starts off the circulation and produces the life of man. Therefore, there is something behind it all which . we are ignoring when we are eternally looking at our own reflection in the mirror of nature. We have, strange to say, recognized the extraordinary character of the universe, its illimit-ability, the fact that space is infinite and beyond our comprehension, that the theory of motion itself is beyond our comprehension. Nevertheless, the principles of conduct move us to an immediate and final consideration, without giving to them in any sense that which we would give to them in reference to these eternal principles to which I have referred. If we are circumscribed within the confines of this narrow sphere within which we live, then those principles of utilitarianism which the hon. gentlemen advocates might well be so considered. But it is not so, and when we see that the eternal Creator of it all has laid down an inviolable law which cannot be infringed, which even the youngest child that ever was horn and some indeed that are not born cannot infrirtge without the penalty being exacted mercilessly, it must be apparent that we cannot regard these things as some humane gentlemen pretend to do. The hon. gentleman himself is not so much older than I am, that it would be presumptuous in me to say he has made a mistake in his consideration of life. Life is not a Sunday school, nor is it, for most of us, that easy affair which possibly it has been to him. It is a most serious and awful thing. It is not a comedy nor a drama, but a tragedy. We must bear in mind that life is not to be considered in the light of these humane principles which the hon. gentleman has laid down. If we are to be scientific, we must examine the facts as they are. If we are to be philosophical ,or religious, we must examine the facts as they are. If however, we are simply to be utilitarian without regard to those other two great divisions of thought, we will no doubt follow the course adopted by the hon. gentleman. We will live in places where it is more

offensive to have a hanging or an execution than it is to face the alternatives. If the hon. gentleman lived in a mining camp, where murders were frequently committed, he would at last beyond a doubt be prevailed upon to say, "This must be stopped; the men who have committed these crimes cannot be confined, and because we have no place within which to confine them, so we will have to take them out and shoot them." I shudder also at Hell, not from fear of it, but at the awfulness of it. * From my earliest recollection I have been impressed with the view that capital punishment should not be exercised in any country in the world. not to be forgotten, is that of giving. the individual an opportunity of reformation. That is not a light matter. The next point is the reformation of the individual. This may be called sentimental. . If there be joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, is it not worth while that the Parliament of the Dominion of Canada should give several sinners each year full opportunity for repentance?
