I was pleased to see to-day on the floor of the House a former member of the Ontario Government, and I am of the opinion that if he could have spoken his mind in this House this afternoon, his views would have, partially at least, coincided with those of the hon. member for the St. Lawrence division. I had the honour of preceding as Provincial Secretary of Ontario the Hon. Mr. Hanna, and my predecessor was the late Mr. Stratton, who.had
the idea that the Central Prison at Toronto should be removed from the centre of that city and that different treatment should be meted out to those sent up for less than two years. I was very strongly of the same view. When the Hon. Mr. Hanna came into office, he proceeded along lines of prison reform, and the very same arguments that I have heard here this afternoon in favour of capital punishment were uttered against his propositions for prison reform. He took the ground, after full investigation in some of the states of the Union where the methods of dealing with criminals have been greatly revised, where capital punishment has been abolished, that there was a better method of treating our unfortunate brethren than by the utmost severity of the law. He took the viewpoint expressed a moment ago by myself, that if there was something good \in humanity it should be cultivated, and that it was the duty of the state not to crush out with an iron hand what is good, but to give it an opportunity to develop, and sooner or later, in the majority of cases, the man whom we formerly looked upon as a criminal might become a benefit and even an ornament to society. He established the prison farm system, and the prisoners do the work of the ' ordinary farmer; out of doors engaged in healthy occupation. They are not only improving themselves physically, but they are earning for the State and they are producing for their own maintenance as well as for the maintenance of others, and although it is true that occasionally a man does not respect the liberty thus given him, the records of the Province of Ontario will show that this reformation in the treatment of prisoners has been good not only for the individual, but for the State.
From various states of the Union and from other countries have come men to investigate the system of prison reform which is in its early stages in Ontario, with the object of adapting that system in their own country. The very same principle that applies to the treatment of men convicted of minor offences can be applied to the treatment of our unfortunate, yes, vicious fellow men who have committed greater crimes. This advance movement in the mehod of treating criminals may be slow, but leading men of the Dominion, who are not in public life, but who have the keeping of their brethren in their care, men high up in the ministry, men in the professions, thinking business-men, are joining

Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer humble apologies on behalf of that section of our community which obeys the law, which maintains the State, and which, speaking generally, conforms to the rules of life laid down by God and man. It is apparently the view of my hon. friend (Mr. Bicker-dike) that this element of the community is of a negligible character, and the only thing to be considered is the right, interest, and advantage of those who set at defiance the laws of God and man. In my view there is no foundation for the suggestion that the proposal now before the House is in the interest of the sacredness of human life. My emphatic protest against it is that it is an attack upon the saoredness of human life. I have listened to the eloquence of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in regard to the opportunity that should be given to the convicted murderer for reformation. I am here to speak on behalf of the victim, and to ask where does consideration for the victim come in? Where and how does the victim have an opportunity to make his peace with God, who has been hurried into the presence of his Maker by the hand of a murderer? You say, but the murder has been done. That is true, but murders are done to-day, and other murders are done to-morrow, and the obligation is laid upon the members of this House, representing the people of Canada, to see that such measures are placed upon the statute book and such administration given as will secure as far as possible, that no man, woman or child shall be hurried unprepared into the presence of their Maker by the hand of a murderer.
I was somewhat touched by the suggestion that those who are not in favour of the murderer as against the murdered are therein non-progiressive. Permit me to point out that all that has been argued here to-day was argued thousands of years ago amongst many savage tribes, and amongst many tribes (the principle still prevails to-day that a murder can be condoned by the payment jyt money. Surely ithiat de ia much better primuiple than destroying tlie life of the murderer, better than placing the murderer in duress at the expense of the state? We are not going forward when we are heading to the condition

of savagery which prevailed thousands of years ago, as history tells us and which prevails to-day, as we know of our own knowledge.
It is a question of stupendous importance; it touches the heart and mind of every responsible member of Parliament, of every man charged with responsibility in connection with the matter, and I certainly want to discharge my duty, as our Mends here want to discharge theirs. It is an easy way of escaping responsibility-and this is the logic <of the attitude taken-to say that the murder having been committed the only question to be considered is the good of the murderer. I submit that the question to be considered is the future good of society and of the State, and if it should unfortunately be the case that the good of the murderer does not run on all fours with the good of the State, then in my humble judgment so much the worse for the murderer. His was the choice not the unfortunate victim's. The State has to consider the question of the greatest good to the greatest number, and I submit that that question is decided by taking such a course as shall tend in the largest possible measure to protect the interests of the law-abiding section <of the community against the passion or rapacity or other evil desires that may !be conjured up by those who are not of a law-abiding character. It has been stated that some pf the .states of the Union have declared against capital punishment. 1 am sorry I am not as familiar with the course of history in the neighbouring republic as some of our friends seem to be. I am somewhat familiar with recent history, hpwever, and I would ask whether the state of California ,is one of those that have abolished capital punishment.
Not yet.

Because I recall that at
the time of the San Francisco earthquake advantage was taken of that terrible tragedy by the criminally inclined to commit murders and robbery, and under the authority of the Governor of the state, so I am credibly informed, the late General .Funston posted soldiers in the streets with orders to shoot on sight any one caught in the act of robbing a .body, or pillaging of any kind. Who will say that that was not a wise and humane course to take? Or are those states in which we read of lynehings *taking place, the states that have declared against capital punishment?
No.

Well, I aiu here to make this argument Wherever an aggrieved c;ti-zcn or family few that substantial justice cannot be expected at the hands of authority, then under the law of God that is planted in the heart of man, the law will be taken in the hands of those that are aggrieved. That is the lynch law that prevails and has prevailed for ages throughout the United States. There is no state of the Union today where it does not prevail on occasion. I do not think there is any example that can be drawn from history, recent or ancient, that will prove that those who commit the most terrible oflence against humanity should not be dealt with according to the laws laid down in Scripture and implanted by the Divine Power in the heart of mankind.
Hon. WM. PUGSLEY. (St. John City): I desire to say a very few words upon this question. I agree that the measure introduced by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) is one of very great importance, and deserving, I think, of the very serious consideration of this House. I notice that a difference of opinion has been expressed as to what has taken place in other countries which have done away with capital punishment. My hon. friend the Solicitor General stated that he knew of countries which had adopted legislation abolishing capital punishment, but which had gone back to the law as they had it before. That statement was denied by my hon. friend who has introduced this Bill, and I am inclined to think that my hon. friend from St. Lawrence is in the right, and that there are very few, if any, countries, that have taken what is regarded by a great many people, and myself among the number, as a forward movement, and have afterwards reversed their action. I think the measure is one that ought fairly to go to a special committee to investigate the results of similar legislation in other countries, more particularly in the United States. I am inclined to think that the records will show that, so far from the abolition of capital punishment leading to an increase of crime, the effect has been quite the reverse. I am inclined to think that those persons who commit murder have but little regard to the consequences to themselves; I doubt if many who have in their hearts the desire to do murder are deterred by the knowledge that the penalty may be the loss of their own lives.

Mr. Speaker, kindly allow me a few remarks ament the question mow before the House. The subject is of the greatest importance and deserving of our very earnest consideration. Every year the House is called upon to pronounce on this proposition, which our learned friend brings forward with characteristic perseverance, study and energy. I do not intend this evening to repeat all the arguments which I have had the opportunity already of bringing to bear in this debate, I merely wish to call attention to a few points, the House having long ago heard the pro and con "of this important discussion. Any lengthy remarks on my part would be out of place.
First of all, I may be permitted to reply to the honourable and learned member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) who, when this question was last debated, took me to task because I did not share his views. My object in taking the floor is to reply to the unfair references of the learned member. He states I am in favour of capital punishment because the more hangings, the better for me. That is quite uncalled for, and the distinguished member in speaking thus was most unfair.

What benefit does a Crown attorney reap when cases of capital punishment increase in number? That does not add to his fees? What interest can the legal representative of the Crown have in the matter? None whatever. Our grief is profound and our misgivings many when we have to insist on the daw taking its course after a jury has brought in a verdict of guilty against am individual. How deep our regret when we have to move for a sentence of death! How cautiously we proceed! First of all the facte are investigated by men quite competent and wise. They decide as to whether any one is liable to prosecution. Then the grand jury takes the matter in hand, and no precaution is overlooked that may prevent a possible mistake. Yes, I reiterate my statement, nothing is neglected and in case of doubt, if we are not fully convinced of the guilt of the accused, we instruct the jury to render a verdict in favour of the prisoner. People are fond of talking against miscarriages of justice, miscarriages that never have taken place. It has been stated that an Italian who. had been adjudged guilty and wras reprieved' later on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice had been the victim of a judicial error. I was Crown prosecutor at the first trial. The jury failed to agree and the case was postponed to the next assizes. The prisoner claimed that he had not produced all his witnesses and -taken advantage of all his privileges. For those xeiasons we adjourned his case to the next term so as to give him an opportunity of preparing his defence. His means being insufficient to allow him to bring his witnesses to court, the Crown undertook to pay their conduct-money. So we obtained the evidence of witnesses whom he claimed would testify on his behalf, but their testimony went against him and'left no doubt as to his guilt. Later on, after serving a term in gaol, he was sentenced to hang, but the Minister of Justice thought fit to recommend his enlargement. I do not blame the hon. the minister but there had certainly been no miscarriage of justice. The guilt had been established beyond all doubt, but certain parties who had testified against the prisoner thought fit for one reason or another to swear to an affidavit that might justify the Minister of Justice setting him free. Again I say there had been no error, but the pardon was a mere act of clemency on the part of the minister.
It has been said and repeated on all occasions that capital punishment is absolutely ineffective and does not act as a deterrent; that it is too severe, and should
be abolished; that the laws of humanity do not countenance the infliction of the sentence of death on human being. Quite easy to argue and quite easy to bring to pass. My observation, however, and my experience have fully satisfied me that since the infliction of the death penalty on murderers, there has been a marked decrease in the number of murders.
One can easily make the statement that the extreme penalty is no deterrent; but I claim that if capital punishment be done away with, crime will increase a hundredfold. Many criminally inclined wisely fear the scaffold, and were confinement the only punishment, many more among them would become murderers. It has been urged that it is wrong and inhuman to take the lives of the culprits; but when assassins; bandits and murderers kill; when they strike right and left, who among them has ever stayed his hand, impelled by like consideration for hte victim? Murderers find time to effect their reconoidiaition with society and make their peace with their own conscience and with God. They have ample opportunity to arrange their domestic matters, while the victims they- have ushered unprepared into eternity without a moment's notice may not have had the opportunity of making preparation, of putting their affairs in order, -and) especially making themselves ready for the life eternal.	-
Well, my opinion, Mr. Speaker, is that such an argument takes into account only one side of the question. Had this mode of dealing with criminals not been attempted elsewhere, were we without any experience from other countries, we might perhaps say: Let us do away with capital punishment and judge of the results in the next few years to come. But the experiment has been tried and the states which introduced the new system had to return to the old, on account of the large increase in crime.
I am quite aware that no reasoning on my part will convince any of the hon. members who have taken sides on this question; and it is far from my thought, quite far indeed, to say anything that may stand in the way of my hon. friend's efforts.
Should his proposition prevail, so much the better for him; and if I could anywise help him, I should do it -quite heartily. What could I deny the hon. member from St. Lawrence? He is an old friend of mine, a generous man, an old fighter who always answered the call when his services were required. Were my convictions different, I should be the first to side with him; but it is a matter of conscience with me to raise my voice against this Bill.
Intentionally?

It is the plea of the young man himself that the shooting of Mrs. Vincent was accidental, but he is the only one who says so. He made no attempt at all to render any assistance to the woman after she was shot. When the husband came home he took the first opportunity to shoot him too. He shot him, rendering

him unconscious, and then he went and got a shot gun, blew the man's head off, got the money and got away with it. Yet, we are asked to believe that the shooting of Mrs. Vincent was accidental.
I do not understand that the enforcement of the death penalty is a matter of vengeance. The law, I believe, is administered for the purpose of preventing the perpetration of crimes of this character. If there ever was a case calling for very careful consideration by council I would think it would be this one. I am not going to discuss the general principles of the Bill submitted by my hon. friend. There is room for discussion both ways. There is no doubt that there are cases in which there are extenuating circumstances, where murders are committed hastily, where, for instance, a man in a passion will lift up a gun or an axe and take another man's life. These are cases in which there might be some jurisdiction for granting a reprieve, but careful consideration must be given when it is evident that a coldblooded murder has been committed after having been planned, no doubt as this murder must have been planned, by this young man. They claim he is only sixteen years of age. I have not been in the district since this murder was committed, but I have letters from my friends there who claim that the boy is over twenty years and that he has the appearance of a man. I think that indicates that he is much older than he claims to be. But, whether he is sixteen years of age or not, he had been working for some years in the district, he was thoroughly responsible and knew what he was doing, and if crimes of this kind are to be committed in this country without punishment such as the law provides. I have very grave doubts as to the country being able to maintain its proud boast that it has never had a lynching. Why? Simply because the law has been administered. If a man was guilty of murder he was almost sure to suffer the penalty provided for the offence. When I went to the West some thirty years ago gamblers used to come across from the other side of the line. The red-coated mounted police were patrolling the boundary in southern Manitoba and when these gamblers would fall out, one would say to the other: If I had you over on the other side of the line I would blow your brains out. Why did they not do it on this side of the line?-because they knew that if they did it they would suffer the death penalty.
Was there not capital punishment on the other side?

There was, but, unfortunately, the law was not administered as it was here. With reference to this murder of which I have spoken, I hope that this application will receive very careful consideration at the hands of the Government, as all matters of that kind must. It is a very serious matter to take the life of any man either by law or otherwise, but I firmly believe that if capital punishment were done away with there would be more lives taken in this country than there are at the present time.
There is no question but that the fear of the gallows has saved' many a man's life. Everybody dm the western country knows that this is the case and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) who spoke so feelingly, knows that it is true. I am not bloodthirsty enough to wish to take any man's life. I heard the hon. member for St. John (M.r. Pugsley) a few moments ago make the statement that the taking of a life by. larw would not do any
9 p.m. good to the party who had been murdered. I agree with my hon. friend thoroughly, but the law was not designed as a matter of vengeance, or to do any good to the party murdered. It was designed to set an example, to deter others from committing the same crime that the condemned person was suffering for. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) made an eloquent appeal. I sympathize with the sentiments expressed by the hon. gentlemen who are advocating this bill, but, there is no analogy between the prison reforms that are taking place in Ontario and in other parts of this great continent, or between men who have committed some petty crime and found their way into the penitentiary, and a coldblooded murder where a man premeditates a crime and gees out and deliberately murders another.
Another argument advanced by these hon. gentlemen is that you are ushering a man into eternity without giving him an opportunity to prepare. That is a sound argument, but what about that man and woman who were ushered into eternity by this young man without a moment's notice? They were given no time to prepare. It might as well have been their own son that committed that murder as the man who did it because he was treated as a member of the family. What about the children, the orphans, the brothers and sisters left to mourn the death of their

parents? If this crime is not punished according to our present law, what is there to prevent other crimes being committed by men of this stamp? We have had several cases in that western country of young English boys coming out and committing horrible crimes.
N.ot English boys.

English boys from the Bernardo school-more than half a dozen cases of them. It is a serious question and one that ought to be weighed very seriously bj every member of this House before voting for a bill that would in any way lessen the penalty for murder. In view of that fact, in view of the murder that has been [DOT] committed among my own friends, and the possibility that this matter will come before the Government on an application for a reprieve and that petitions have been largely signed all over the country-for it is no trouble to get a petition of this kind signed, as people become hysterical on such occasions and thousands and thousands of people will sign it who know nothing at all about the evidence, who do not weigh the matter but simply sign the petition because they think it is kindly and right thing to ask for the life of this young man- I take the position I have taken. I do not intend to say anything more on this Bill and would not have spoken if this case had not been brought forward as one reason why a Bill of this kind should be passed. This is a case which I think should emphasize the necessity of keeping the law just as it is, leaving the law to take its course.

I have no right to
further intervene in the debate, having spoken once. I simply rise to refer to the request of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to allow the Bill to pass the second reading and be submitted to a committee of the House, and to give my reason foi the position I think the House should take. He based his request upon the fact that a statement of mine to the effect that there have been countries in Europe, if not States in the American Republic, which had abolished capital punishment and afterwards reverted to it, was denied by the hon. member for the St. Lawrence division (Mr. Bickerdike), and that consequently there was a state of disputed facts that might well be submitted to a committee.
I do not think that a very strong case could be made for a submission to a committee on so narrow a dispute on facts as that. I observe this, and I had it in mind at the time I was speaking before, that in the debate in 1915 the Minister of Justice referred to several countries as in the category

I described. He referred to Austria-Hungary as having abolished capital punishment and having again returned to that treatment of murderers, and asserted as a fact that this had been the case. He referred also to the cases of Brunswick, Cobourg, Nassau, and Oidenburg which abolished capital punishment in 1849; Saxe-Meiningen and Saxe-Weimar in 1862 and Baden in 1863 and to Saxony which abolished it in 1868, all of whom returned to capital punishment under the Imperial Criminal Code of 1872. He referred further to the case of Russia who abolished capital punishment in 1850 and again returned to it, and for many years continued the practice of capital punishment.
Then repealed it again.

Not altogether. But
even if they ihad it would still be a case of a country that had abolished capital punishment and returned to it and so would come within the class to which I referred. It is true that in 1907 capital punishment was again abolished in Russia, and again I am relying upon the minister's statement, which he says he very carefully affirmed. He says that while it was abolished in 1907 it was not wholly abolished, but was retained only for the offence of the murder of the Emperor or Empress of Russia or the heir to the throne. It may be. that under the newer conditions that now obtain in Russia the lives of the people generally may be considered as sacred as those of the Emperor or Empress and the heir to the throne. He referred also to certain .states of the American Union as hawing long ago abolished capital punishment and having then found the error of their ways. He referred to Rhode Island, Colorado and the state of Maine, and said:
It is true, some of these states have since abolished it again. But, so far as the hon. gentleman seems to find what he regards as an unanswerable argument in the fact that that those states that have abolished capital punishment have, never repented their action.
Those are cases, several of them in Europe especially, where there has been reversion, that is where capital punishment once abolished was afterwards restored. I have read the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence division following the Minister of Justice. I have read his speech again in 1916, and I listened to his speech to-day; but I have seen nothing to contradict the individual instances given by the Minister of Justice. I shall not refer to the subject further than to eay that if I have observed the course of the debate cor-

rectly I do not think that the sense of this House is to the effect that there should be any serious intention on the part of this Parliament at this time to abolish capital punishment. The discussion is well worth while, but it would be saying too much to gather from this debate that there appears to be a sense of the House looking to a serious consideration of its abolition now. I think myself the vote of the second reading might well take place.

I presume I shall
be expected to Teply to some of the very unjust criticisms that have been offered to the Bill which I introduced. I would say to my good friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) that the statement I made was this, that no country or no state in the world that had abolished capital punishment had resumed it at the present time.
Resumed it since.

Resumed it at the
present time. I know that there were some cases, as in Russia, which, as my hon. friend said, abolished capital punishment for everything except the murder of the crowned heads.
What about those states in Germany?

I have some doubt
about them. But it may be possible that Austria-Hungary, from some things that they have done recently, would return to capital puishment. But I do not think that our House should follow .them.
Would the hon. member prefer to follow the examples he has cited or those in Great Britain and France?
I would prefer to follow Russia just now.
Yes, I thought so.

I hope that within a week this House will send a cable to Petrograd congratulating Russia on having abolished capital punishment entirely, and also upon the removal of all .German influences in that country.
My good friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) has undertaken to say that that young man was guilty of murder. I have in my possession ten thousand or fifteen thousand signatures of people who say he was not.
He was found guilty by the trial judge.
Found guilty by the jury and sentenced by Judge Macdonald- and I hope Judge Macdonald will be ashamed of himself for doing so.

speechtext: Order. I hope the hon. member does not mean to cast any reflection upon the Bench, because he would be distinctly out of order in doing so.

Well, may I express my opinion about the jury? I still say that I am ashamed of him, if he is not ashamed of himself. I am sure there is not any man in Canada, in this House or out of it, who would stand for hanging a woman or a child, notwithstanding what my leader said this afternoon. I cannot believe it possible that a man who is a man would stand foT hanging a woman or a child, and I do not think that any of those who have spoken to-day would do so. They might give somebody else thirty pieces of silver to go and do it, but they would not do it themselves. The right hon. leader of the Opposition spoke of President Fallieres this afternoon. I think that President Fallieres was the greatest and best man that France ever produced. What did President Failures say? He said that if the judges who condemned a man to death had to do the hanging, there would be no more hanging. I have a better suggestion than that, I should like to see my good friend the leader of the Opposition and my good friend the member for West Peterborough do the hanging. I think that under those conditions hanging would soon stop.
I have seen men whom I would hang with pleasure.

I have not the
slightest doubt of that. Any man who would stand up in this House and say he wanted to hang that boy would do almost anything.
I did not say that.

The eix-Mindster of
Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) said that he was very much pleased that justice in Canada was administered in such a just and equitable manner. I question very much whether he was correct in that view. I knew a man not four hundred miles from Montreal who stole a horse and buggy. He was sentenced to penitentiary for two years, persecuted right to the end by the man he stole the horse and buggy from, while the man he stole the horse and buggy from stole a whole -railroad and- burst a bank-and he was knighted. I think your

whole system of punishment is wrong. You should punish with a view to making better men and women when you put them into prison. You punish for revenge, but you have no authority from Scripture to punish at aid. There is not a verse in the word of God from Genesis to Revelation that gives you authority to punish a man at all or to hang him. I challenge the whole House to find it.
There is no use appeal-iny to the other side; they are not familiar with the Scriptures.
I asked you about hell.

The member for
Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) apologized for what he was doing. What do they say in France-qui s'excuse s'accuse? He said he was sorry when he had to hang these men; it pains him very much-but he takes the pay all the same. It is blood money, but, like Pilate of old, he washes his hands of it and turns jfrover to the jury, asking them to be merciful-after saying everything he could against the prisoner.
The Minister of Justice said that he had divine sanction for hanging these poor criminals and sending their souls into eternity. I challenged him then to produce that authority, and I challenge him now to do so. The Minister has no divine mandate to hang a boy. If he has such a mandate, it should be placed on the Table of the House so that members on each side may examine it, so that it may be incorporated in the Canadian Archives, to enable generations yet unborn to realize that in the year 1917 there was in the Canadian Government a Minister of Justice who had divine authority for hanging a boy. With all due respect to the Minister of Justice, his extravagant utterances on this subject could have been inspired only by a prejudice. Take the case of self-defence. I contend that only in self-defence, if at all, are we justified in taking human life.
Conceiving that a man has the right under natural instinct and statutory laws to kill another in self-defence, can any man establish self-defence by shooting another who was known to be as helpless as if handcuffed with his hands behind his back? Then, it is no better in principle for the state to do this than it is for a citizen. Society has no more right to trifle with the most sacred work of God than the individual has. The minister sends a young 'boy, handcuffed and guarded by the police, from a modern penitentiary of cement, granite, steel and armour plate, takes him out

upon the gallows and hangs him until he is dead. Surely my friends won't say that that boy was hanged in self-defence.
I ask the hon. gentleman, since he draws so much upon his vivid imagination-
That is no imagination. The boy is condemned there in Winnipeg-
-regarding the horrors of condemning this young man to death-
This child.
May I ask the hon. gentlemen, then, how he escapes condemning the work of the Creator in condemning to eternal punishment a man who had committed a sin like that?

That is too deep for me; I give it up. It is a question that would require a notice of motion. Seven and one-half millions against one poor unfortunate fellow locked up in a penitentiary -and yet you say you are going to hang him in self-defence. I should like very much to touch the heart of the Solicitor General. I know it is difficult. I mentioned a case last session, and as I think he did not grasp it, I submit again that where the equities are equal, the element of mercy should hold the balance of power in deciding this question-the awful suffering and remorse of the family of the victim of a homicide. I agree that it is hard on the family of the deceased, and my sympathy goes out to them. Whether his death was the result of an assassination or a justifiable homicide, it is all the same to them. But, for that reason, would you have two widows, two sets of orphans, and two sorrowing parents? I do not think that capital punishment does any good. The family of the prisoner are just as innocent of an offence as the family of the deceased, and are just as much entitled to compassion and sympathy. For example, a man commits murder. He probably got drunk, or was by environment made a criminal. He has a good wife and also children; a good mother and father, and a large number of relatives, all innocent people, and profoundly grieved that the offense was committed. The accused is tried, convicted, and sentenced to be hanged. The very thought of taking the life of the husband, father, brother and son breaks a multitude of hearts. The time has healed the wounds that grief for the victim rent, but as the

days roll by and the time approaches for the execution of the prisoner, the heart of the mother and the father all but breaks, the affectionate and tender cord of love that stretches from the altar to the scaffold is crushed hut not broken, and the heart of the wife is burned to its very socket. She goes tp and from the awful death cell. Little innocent hearts of children are crushed like the tender blades of grass beneath the angry heels of cannon on the German battlefield, yet they are all innocent. The brother and sister suffer for his sins, and see his ghost-like form in their dreams of repose. As the day draws.near, the father and mother with tittering footsteps visit the death cell, and their minds wander back to the time when a little boy said his prayers at his mother's knee, and they ask God why they have this affliction to hear. The wife, children, relatives and friends all bid Ihiim good-bye and leave with breaking hearts, bitterly thinking of tomorrow. With 'heart-breaking despair, the mother prays Gpd to spare her son, and as , the time flies by the height of Heaven could not measure her sorrow. The father's hair turns gray over night, and the very souls are all scarred and forever seared over by the thought of the vengeance visited on their unfortunate relative, son and husband .and father. The parents are hurried to itheir graves; by broken hearts; the wife tries to forget, but cannot forgive; and the hearts of the children, relatives 'and friends are hardened by the harrowing example of killiflg by the State. Two families are in mourning, and the prisoner's family crushed and heart-broken by a protracted suspense, and that amounts to cruelty to the innocents. Then why make two families instead of one desolate.
Then, suppose he was innocent? There have been oases-we have hiad such cases right here: dri Oamada-of ibnooenlt men, being hanged:. There was such a case molt long ago in the United States, and I will mention others before I get through. The State cannot retract what it has done. If life imprisonment would serve the same purpose, would you not prefer iit to1 (the death penalty?
It is this spirit which must modify the law. Even if hell and death alike were -necessary to be emphasized as penalties for the wicked in more barbarous ages, it is heaven and life which are to be chiefly taught as rewards for the good in the better and gentler days that are dawning. And this expresses a similar view to that maintained by the most competent judges, that
pushing the death penalty only makes it worthless as a deterrent in communities that have reached the state of settled obedience to law.
It appears to me, therefore, to be in harmony with the highest teaching of life that if the death penalty be the greatest deterrent in Canada in the twentieth century, then Christianity has not succeeded in influencing men's thoughts as much as the so-called pagan pre-Christian philosophers of Rome. They had so prepared men's minds and developed men's characters that the death penalty was able to be -abolished in Rome within five hundred years of Rome being founded, whereas some of our judges on the bench and most of our Christian bishops to-day in England say that capital punishment should not be abolished because it is the most powerful deterrent.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) spoke about this young man who had committed murder. To hear the hon. gentleman talk you would think that there was no capital punishment in Manitoba, and that it was for that reason that this crime took place. But that is not the case at all, for capital punishment is the law for Manitoba. I hope it will not be so for long.
Theoretically, from a contemplation of the claims of a Christianity exercised for nearly two thousand years, I should have expected that capital punishment would not now be the only and best deterrent from crime, and upon grounds of theory alone I should have felt justified in advocating that England, the professed pioneer in our humanitarian reforms, should have . been willing to set the great example to the world of abolishing capital punishment as the proof of the sincerity of her claim. She has, however, lost that honour. Others have preceded her in the field, and with more matured faith in human nature and in the progress of culture, have removed its stigma from their statute-books. The result has been so thoroughly satisfactory, and the success has been so commensurate with the state of cultured civilization, that Canada has no excuse for now holding back ' from the same step, unless she is willing to stand self-convicted of a lower civilization and of a more perpetuated brutality than those nations who have found themselves fit to be freed from the yoke of death.
If Canada is lower in civilization than the countries wherein capital punishment has been successfully abolished, where is the boasted value of the freedom of her institutions, of her religion, of the development of her humanity and of her culture?

Any sufficiently civilized country that has enough faith may fearlessly abolish capital punishment from her statute-book. The actual valuelessness of capital punishment as a deterrent, and of its evil effect as an incentive to induce similar crimes, is to be gathered from the records of every land.
With the progress of civilization the inviolability of human life is more and more recognized. _The idea of the dignity of man, of the inviolability of life even in the newborn child, is derived from Christianity, and a higher civilization must seek to 'proclaim it in legislation. But each execution speaks a different language. It proclaims in a loud voice to the crowd assembled round the scaffold that the State does not consider itself bound to respect human life, and that it regards itself as authorized to db that Which is a crime in the individual.
My hon. friend from Edmonton said that there was Scripture authority for hanging. I maintain that there is no such authority. But there is a commandment which says "Thou shalt not kill;" and all the legislation in the country will never get the "not" out of that commandment. That applies to the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) as well as the leader of the Opposition and the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). That commandment was given amidst the thunders of Sinai. It does not say that the state may kill and that the individual must not; that the state may. murder a man but that the individual must not murder. There are no exceptions to that law.

How does the hon.
member then make an exception?
I do not.

The hon. gentleman
makes an exception of self-defence.
I say the command is plain-"Thou shalt not kill". Of course, the hon. member (Mr. Burnham) will say that the word "not" should not be there.

The Old Testament Scriptures say "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood 'be shed." And Christ himself when he was being taken, and when Peter drew his sword and cut off the ear of the High Priest's servant, said "They that take the sword shall perish by the sword." What construction does the hon. gentelman put upon these words in the Old Testament Scriptures and in the New?
Mr. BICKERDIKE- It seems to me the matter is very simple. Christ's words

were "They that take the sword shall perish by the sword." But does that mean that all our returned soldiers must be killed? Surely there is no argument jn these words against what I have said. And it is true the Old Testament Scriptures contain the words the hon gentleman (Mr. Ball) has quoted. And thoise words are perfectly true. For that is what has been done, and is being done today even here in Canada. But the "shall" there was not a command but a prophecy.
What word, then, would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) have used?

You find the -same used in the declaration that in the latter days perilous times shall, come. Why, Moses himself was a murderer. He killed the Egyptian with whom he contended. Yet his blood was not shed by man.
What construction do you place upon the words, "They that take the sword shall perish by the sword"?

Why, that means
that the-Lord was opposed to war. There is no other construction possible. Any Sunday-School child will tell you that. The construction is that the law does not approve of killing at all, neither with the sword of Peter nor the sword of anybody else, not even with the sword of the Kaiser.
Christ would not allow even the ear of the murderer to be cut off.

There is a justification for everything I say to-night, because we find that the only letter that was ever written by our Lord Jesus Christ was the one written by Him in the sand when He sat as a jury trying a poor woman who had made a mistake. When He finished He, as if to interpret the letter He had written, said to the woman: Where are thy accusers? and the woman answered him, Sir, there are none. That was the letter supposed to be written in the sand.
What about those people who go into outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth?

The only one that I have seen gnashing his teeth to-day has been my good friend the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). When I hear a minister of the gospel-I am speaking about Protestant	ministerspreaching in the pulpit on Sunday about Jesus Christ's sacrifices and the forgiveness

of sins, and on Monday advocating capital punishment and revenge, I say that he is neither more nor less than a sounding brass and tinkling cymbal, and I ask the old question: Was it he or his parents who sinned? for that man was certainly born blind.
May I be permitted to quote from a good friend of mine in New York, Mr. Thomas Mott Osborne, one of the greatest authorities on capital punishment on this side of the Atlantic, if not in the world. He says:
Certainly we ought to be in no way behind Russia in conserving human life. There is no question as this one of capital punishment which calls for plain common sense in dealing with it. It is not an abstruse question. The ridiculous thing we do in prisons with our prisoners will not bear being brought to light. For instance, what is the advantage in shaving the heads of prisoners? What is the use of treating a man in such a way that he is stamped as a convict when he goes back into civil life? I plead for this question to be approached in a reasonable and intelligent manner without trace of hysteria. There is no doubt that a lot of men are in prison who ought not to be there, but it is equally true that there are a lot who are not there and ought to be there.
Perhaps my hon. friend who was knighted might be amongst them. Mr. Osborne goes on to say:	,
It is not advisable to get sentimental about the men in prison, for in all my experience I have discovered only two men whom I thought were really innocent and ought not be in prison.
The whole question of capital punishment must be viewed from the point of the advantage of society.
It is no use discussing that question from any other point of view in any country.
If it is for the advantage of society that men ought to be killed, then let them be killed.
But we have first of all to see that it is for the advantage of society. If it is for the advantage and protection of society that men should be killed, let us kill them; but if not, let us not do so.
Equally, if it Is to the advantage of society that a .man should be shackled for life, then let him be shackled. The advantage and interests of society must be the first consideration. As with a man who has the smallpox. You send him to the hospital and quarantine him. not only to protect society, but also to *protect himself.
That is what we do when we send a man to penitentiary for life.
The certainty of punishment is far more effective than the magnitude of it. A man will be in more fear of punishment if he knows that when found guilty the hand of the
law will certainly fall upon him, and exact the penalty. That is clearly seen in the punishment of our own children. It is also proved by statistics. In the state of Maine capital punishment has been abolished, re-Tntroduced and abolished again, with the result that there has been a greater percentage of convictions with the absence of capital punishment than with it. A jury is not so ready to convict a man if they know that the penalty will be death, blit they will find a man guilty more often if the punishment is a mere nominal one. The statistics for the state of Maine show that when capital punishment was in force only 27 per cent of convictions followed the indictments. When it was removed that number increasid to 59 per cent. Wren capital punishment was re-introduced the figure dropped to 30 per cent., and when it was abolished again the number increased to 60' per cent, thus showing that there are a greater number of convictions with the absence of capital punishment.

Maine was one of the states that the minister said had abolished capital punishment and had reinstated it.
I see it has abolished it again.

Does the hon. member overlook the fact that some of the states abolished capital punishment because the citizens wished to have the privilege of killing people without being punished for it? You will find that to be the case in some remote districts.

Mr. Osborne goes on to say:
I personally have put more men to death than any other man in the United States. I have executed forty men during my term or two and a half years as warden of Sing Sing prison. I did not attend the executions, and on all occasions except two I was absent from the prison as a protest. But there is not a man who has anything to do with executions directly who does not hate it.
There is also the uncertainty of execution which has a great influence on crime.
He goes on to prove that of the criminals condemned in the state of New York only about 1.3 per cent were executed. He goes on to say:
It is claimed that capital punishment frightens people from committing crime, and because of fear they will refrain from murder. But where is there a man worth his salt who will change his line of conduct because of a fear of punishment? I have never yet found a crook who is frightened by the severity of the law. There might be a few cowards outside who are prevented from murder by fear of the chair. But the example of the state makes murderers. There are boys in the' underworld who regard the men who go to the chair as heroes, and there is not one man who goes to the chair who does not go there bravely and ready to meet his fate. For every man you put to death, there are six boys ready to spring up in his place. The



fear of punishment is not a deterrent. There are two kinds of a murderer-one who commits a crime in the heat of passion or when enraged by liquor, and the other who deliberately plans a murder and who a'so at the same time plans his escape from the law.
It has been conceded by some of the most eminent physicians that any man committing a murder has an unbalanced mind at the moment. At the moment, at least, he is temporarily insane. He may be enraged through a sense of being wronged, or through kindred emotions, and is in no mood to weigh the results of his acts, or to take account of punishments confronting him. It is sad to believe that much of the prejudice in favour of the gallows may be traced to three discreditable sources. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) has cited those.
Let me close by saying that capital punishment, although sanctioned by the letter of the old Biblical law, is contrary to its interpretation in the light of Christianity.
